The MEMIT paper proposes a method for directly editing factual associations stored in the weights of large transformer language models such as GPT, allowing modifications to be made without retraining the entire model[^1]. It generalizes the ROME technique by enabling thousands of edits simultaneously, distributing parameter updates across multiple layers rather than confining them to a single layer[^2].

Running a full‑scale LLM on a device with only a few hundred megabytes of RAM is generally not feasible[^1]. However, several compression techniques can shrink the memory requirements enough to run on hardware with 2–4 GB of RAM[^2]. For example, 4‑bit quantization and CPU‑offload pipelines (such as those provided by bitsandbytes or GPTQ) have been shown to enable inference on smartphones with under 1 GB of RAM, though at reduced speed[^3]. Additionally, models specifically designed for tiny footprints—like DistilBERT, TinyLlama, or MobileBERT—can fit under 100 MB and even run on microcontrollers with only a few megabytes of RAM[^4].

ROME edits the model by applying a linear transformation to the weight matrices[^1]. MEMIT modifies the model by adding an activation vector to the residual stream[^2]. Both techniques aim to change model behavior without full fine‑tuning, but they differ in their underlying mechanisms and the scope of changes they can reliably produce[^3].
